subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Gallbladder carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the gallbladder, often linked to chronic inflammation from gallstones or porcelain gallbladder. Genetic mutations (e.g., KRAS, TP53) drive malignant transformation, and early detection is difficult.

sections.p: Gallbladder carcinoma (GBC) is the most common cancer of the extra‑hepatic biliary tree, typically presenting in the seventh decade and slightly more often in women.
b: Incidence rises with chronic gallstone disease.
Porcelain gallbladder confers a high risk.

sections.p: Repeated mechanical irritation and inflammation from stones or parasites cause DNA damage in gallbladder epithelium, leading to dysplasia and carcinoma.
b: Oxidative stress from bile stasis generates mutagenic ROS.
Chronic infection (e.g., Salmonella, Clonorchis) adds carcinogenic nitrosamines.

sections.p: Key pathways altered in GBC include KRAS‑MAPK, TP53‑p21, and EGFR signaling, which control cell proliferation, apoptosis, and DNA repair.
Genetic hits accumulate on a background of chronic inflammation, producing an infiltrating or fungating tumor that invades the liver, liver hilum, and regional nodes.
b: Infiltrating growth spreads to liver segments IVb/V.
Fungating masses may cause biliary obstruction.
Metastasis often to peritoneum and lungs.

sections.p: Patients present with vague right‑upper‑quadrant pain, weight loss, or jaundice from biliary obstruction; early disease is often missed, leading to poor prognosis.
b: Molecular profiling guides targeted therapy (e.g., EGFR inhibitors).
Low‑resource settings rely on clinical suspicion and basic imaging.

t.b: Detects gallbladder wall thickening or mass; a hyperechoic mass suggests carcinoma.
Staging – assesses local invasion and distant spread.
Supports diagnosis; markedly elevated levels raise suspicion.

sections.p: Focus on risk factors, typical genetic alterations, and the staging system (TNM). Remember that gallstones are a modifiable risk.
b: TNM stage I: tumor confined to gallbladder wall.
Stage II: invasion into liver or perimuscular tissue.
Stage III/IV: nodal or distant metastasis.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained weight loss and palpable gallbladder

faq.q: Why are gallstones a risk for cancer?
faq.a: They cause chronic irritation and inflammation, leading to DNA damage and dysplasia.
Early cholecystectomy for large or long‑standing stones reduces risk.
No; it is supportive but not specific enough for screening.

exam: List the major genetic mutations associated with gallbladder carcinoma and their pathogenic role.
Describe the TNM staging criteria for gallbladder cancer.
Explain why chronic gallstone disease predisposes to carcinoma and how this influences management.
